extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive manual of style rules for punctuation, apostrophes, dashes, parentheses, brackets, ellipses, hyphens, and rules for dividing words (including foreign-language-specific division). Intended to guide copy editors and typesetters in preparing scholarly and general prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma with coordinate clauses governing a following clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more co-ordinate clauses ending in a word governing or modifying another word in a following clause should be separated by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “. . . a shallow body of water connected with, but well protected from, the open sea”; “He was as tall as, though much younger than, his brother”; long illustrative example showing repeated adjectival clauses separated by commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to separate two numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate two numbers in a sentence (similarly to clause separation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “In 1905, 347 teachers attended the convention”; dates such as “November 1, 1905.” (See also rule 160.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to indicate omission of repeated words
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is employed to indicate the omission, for brevity or convenience, of a word or words the repetition of which is not essential to the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “In Illinois there are seventeen such institutions; in Ohio, twenty-two; in Indiana, thirteen”; “In Lincoln's first cabinet Seward was secretary of state; Chase, of the treasury; Cameron, of war; and Bates, attorney general.” Note: sometimes such constructions don't require commas if smooth: “One puppy may resemble the father, another the mother, and a third some distant ancestor.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before brief direct quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct quotation, maxim, or similar expression, when brief, should be separated from the preceding part of the sentence by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: “God said, Let there be light.” See also rule 131.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before 'of' for residence or position
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma before 'of' in connection with residence or position (e.g., appositive indicating place or position).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “Mr. and Mrs. McIntyre, of Detroit, Mich.; President Hadley, of Yale University.” Exceptions: historical/political cases where the place-name is effectively part of the name: “Clement of Alexandria, Philip of Anjou, King Edward of England.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma vs en dash for consecutive numbers in references
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references insert a comma between consecutive numbers to represent a break in the continuity, and an en dash to represent one continuous reference between the consecutive numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “pp. 4, 7-8, 10; Ezra 5:7-8; IV, 123-30.” Use en dash for ranges, commas for separate references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma with thousands digits
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma after digits indicating thousands, except in a date or in a page-reference and not between the constituents of dimensions, weights, and measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “1,276, 10,419; 2200 B.C.; p. 2461; 3 feet 6 inches; 4 lb. 2 oz.; 2 hr. 4 min.” Note: Astrophysical Journal and Botanical Gazette do not use a comma with four figures. Note on German/Spanish conventions using period instead of comma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma between month and year
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate month and year and similar time divisions by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “November, 1905; New Year's Day, 1906.” Note: Astrophysical Journal and Botanical Gazette do not use a comma between month and year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit comma after author's name in signatures/headers
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the comma, in signatures and at the beginning of articles, after an author's name followed by address, title, or position in a separate line, or after address followed by a date line, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also rule 65 for related placement guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma placement with quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is always placed inside the quotation marks, but following the parenthesis, if the context requires it at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place comma inside quotes; if parenthesis is present and comma logically applies after parenthesis, put it after the parenthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophe for omission/contractions
rubrics_metrics.description: An apostrophe is used to mark the omission of a letter or letters in the contraction of a word, or of figures in a number. In contractions containing a verb and the negative, do not use a space between the components of the contraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: it's, ne'er, 'twas, 'takin' me 'at'; m'f'g; the class of '96; don't, haven't. See rule 123 for related matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming possessive with apostrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: The possessive case of nouns, common and proper, is formed by the addition of an apostrophe, or apostrophe and s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man's word, horses' tails; Scott's Ivanhoe, Jones's farms, Themistocles' era; for appearance' sake. See rule 113 for cross-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural of numerals and rare coinages using apostrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: The plural of numerals, and of rare or artificial noun-coinages, is formed by the aid of an apostrophe and s; of proper nouns of more than one syllable ending in a sibilant, by adding an apostrophe alone (monosyllabic proper names ending in a sibilant add es; others, s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in the 1900's; in the two's and three's, the three R's, the Y.M.C.A.'s; 'these I-just-do-as-I-please's'; 'all the Tommy Atkins' of England' (but: the Rosses and the Macdougals); the Pericles' and Socrates' of literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dash to denote abrupt break/transition
rubrics_metrics.description: An em dash is used to denote 'a sudden break, stop, or transition in a sentence, or an abrupt change in its construction, a long or significant pause, or an unexpected or epigrammatic turn of sentiment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “Do we — can we — send out educated boys and girls from the high school at eighteen?”; poetic and rhetorical usages illustrating emphasis and dramatic pause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dashes for independent parenthetical interpolations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dashes (rarely parentheses) for parenthetical clauses which are both logically and structurally independent interpolations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This may be said to be — but, never mind, we will pass over that'; longer parenthetical references set off with dashes. See rule 150 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash for emphasis when repeating phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause added to lend emphasis to, or to explain or expand, a word or phrase occurring in the main clause, which word or phrase is then repeated, should be introduced by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'To him they are more important as the sources for history — the history of events and ideas'; 'Here we are face to face with a new and difficult problem — new and difficult, that is, in the sense that ...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash when 'namely' is implied
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever a 'namely' is implied before a parenthetical or complementary clause, a dash should preferably be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'These discoveries — gunpowder, printing-press, compass, and telescope — were the weapons before which the old science trembled'; 'But here we are trenching upon another division of our field — the interpretation of New Testament books.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash before final summarizing clause
rubrics_metrics.description: In sentences broken up into clauses, the final — summarizing — clause should be preceded by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Amos, with the idea that Jehovah is an upright judge . . . ; Hosea, whose Master hated injustice and falsehood . . . ; Isaiah, whose Lord would have mercy only on those who relieved the widow and the fatherless — these were the spokesmen ...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash after run-in side headings/lead-ins
rubrics_metrics.description: A word or phrase set in a separate line and succeeded by paragraphs, at the beginning of each of which it is implied, should be followed by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I recommend — i. That we kill him. 2. That we flay him.' Also: In French and Spanish a dash is used before a speech in direct discourse instead of quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dash with side-heads
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash may be used in connection with side-heads, whether 'run in' or paragraphed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given for topical and side-head use in text layout; see note examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash in place of 'to' connecting words or numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a dash in place of the word 'to' connecting two words or numbers (see rule 158 for ranges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'May–July, 1906' (en dash); 'May 1, 1905 — November 1, 1906' (em dash); 'pp. 3–7' (en dash). But if 'from' precedes the first word or number, do not use the dash instead of 'to' (write 'From May 1 to July 1, 1906'). Also rules on omitting hundreds in consecutive numbers and special B.C. handling. Note about Astrophysical Journal and Botanical Gazette repeating hundreds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash preceding reference after full-sentence quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a dash precede the reference (author, title of work, or both) following a direct quotation, consisting of at least one complete sentence, in footnotes or cited independently in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example footnote format: Quotation — Thirty Years, I, 379. Also an example of a poem line followed by —Emerson, 'To Ellen, at the South.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on dash usage with other punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash should not ordinarily be used in connection with any other point, except a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect: 'DEAR SIR: — I have ...' Correct: 'DEAR SIR: I have ...' Exceptions: retain comma before first dash if that comma would have been necessary without the parenthetical clause; retain interrogation or exclamation points within parenthetical dash-set clauses when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses for enumerations run into text
rubrics_metrics.description: Place between parentheses figures or letters used to mark divisions in enumerations run into the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The reasons for his resignation were three: (1) advanced age, (2) failing health, (3) a desire to travel.' If paragraphed divisions use single parenthesis with lowercase italic letter, period with figures/capital letters. Also recommends notation/indention scheme for syllabi: A., I., 1., a), (1), (a), i), ii), (ft), etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses not preferred for parenthetical clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses should not ordinarily be used for parenthetical clauses unless confusion might arise from the use of less distinctive marks, or unless the content of the clause is wholly irrelevant to the main argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples showing preferred dash usage: 'He meant — I take this to be the (somewhat obscure) sense of his speech — that ...'; 'The contention has been made (op. cit.) that ...' Use parentheses sparingly for asides that are truly irrelevant or likely to confuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brackets uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Brackets are used (1) to inclose an explanation or note, (2) to indicate an interpolation in a quotation, (3) to rectify a mistake, (4) to supply an omission, and (5) for parentheses within parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided for each use: editorial note [—EDITOR.], insertion [the free-silver Democrats], rectifying mistake [Englishman], supplying omitted bibliographic info, and nested bracket use for references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brackets for 'To be continued' style notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases such as 'To be continued' at the end, and 'Continued from ...' at the beginning, of articles, chapters, etc., should be placed between brackets, centered, and set in italics and in reduced type according to reduction rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: [Continued from p. 320], [To be concluded]. See rule 73 and 86 for typography guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses indicate omissions and lacunae
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses are used to indicate the omission, from a quotation, of one or more words not essential to the idea, and also to indicate illegible words, mutilations, and other lacunae in a document, manuscript, or other material quoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an ellipsis at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence use four periods separated by a space (en quad) ordinarily, except in very narrow measures (in French three only, with no space). If preceding line ends in a point, do not include that in the four. When whole paragraphs or lines in poetry are omitted insert a full line of periods separated by em- or 2-em quads; periods should not extend beyond the longest type-line. Numerous examples provided (English and French).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis treated as part of citation
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipsis should be treated as a part of the citation; consequently should be enclosed in the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 178(3) for cross-reference to bracket/quotation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen for line-end division and many compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is placed at the end of a line when the remainder of the last word of which is carried to the next line and between many compound words. Modern tendency favors writing as one or two words when they convey one idea, but many compounds remain better hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: schoolroom, workshop, headquarters. Notes that rules are guidelines and require judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compound adjectives before a noun
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate two or more words (except proper names forming a unity in themselves) combined into one adjective preceding a noun, or into one pronoun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: so-called Croesus, well-known author, first-class investment, better-trained teachers, high-school course, four-year-old boy, up-to-date machinery, deceased-wife's-sister bill; exceptions like New Testament times, Old English spelling, a priori argument. Do not hyphenate adverb+adjective combos when no ambiguity: an ever increasing flood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate noun compounds in objective relation (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate, as a rule, nouns formed by the combination of two nouns standing in objective relation to each other (i.e., one derived from a transitive verb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mind-reader, story-teller, fool-killer, office-holder, well-wisher, property-owner; hero-worship, wood-turning, clay-modeling, curriculum-making. Lists exceptions: common/brief compounds and special meanings like lawgiver, proofreader, waterproof, concussionproof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen with present participle + noun to form new noun
rubrics_metrics.description: A present participle united with a noun to form a new noun with meaning different from the separate words, or with a preposition used absolutely, may properly take a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: boarding-house, dining-hall, sleeping-room, dwelling-place, printing-office, walking-stick, starting-point, stepping-stone, stumbling-block (but meeting place); lean-to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of book, house, mill, room, shop, work general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule, compounds of 'book,' 'house,' 'mill,' 'room,' 'shop,' and 'work' should be printed as one compact word when the prefixed noun contains only one syllable; hyphenated when it contains two; printed as two separate words when it contains three or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples across categories: handbook, schoolbook, notebook; pocket-book, story-book; boathouse, clubhouse, schoolhouse; engine-house, power-house; commill, handmill, sawmill; bedroom, classroom, schoolroom; tinshop, workshop; exceptions include rare combos and those better separated for appearance: wheat mill, school work, home work, class work, book work, team work, source book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate occupation-denoting compounds and adjectival nouns before proper nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'maker,' 'dealer,' and other words denoting occupation should ordinarily be hyphenated; likewise nouns combined in an adjectival sense before a proper noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: harness-maker, book-dealer; a soldier-statesman, the poet-artist Rossetti. Exceptions include short everyday words: bookmaker, dressmaker, shopgirl.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation of 'store' compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'store' should be hyphenated when the prefix contains only one syllable; otherwise not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: drug-store, feed-store (but: bookstore); grocery store, dry-goods store.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'fellow' compounds when first element
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'fellow' are hyphenated when forming the first element of the compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fellow-man, fellow-beings; but: playfellow; 'Mr. Goodfellow'; politics makes strange bedfellows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate kinship-first-element compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'father,' 'mother,' 'brother,' 'sister,' 'daughter,' 'parent,' and 'foster' should be hyphenated when forming the first element of the compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: father-love (but: fatherland), mother-tongue, brother-officer, sister-nation, foster-son, daughter-cells, parent-word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen for 'great-' indicating degree in descent
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'great,' indicating the fourth degree in a direct line of descent, call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: great-grandfather, great-grandson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of 'life' and 'world' require hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'life' and 'world' require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: life-history, life-principle (but: lifetime), world-power, world-problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of 'skin' printed as one or two words by syllable count
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'skin' with words of one syllable are to be printed as one word; with words of more than one, as two separate words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: calfskin, sheepskin; alligator skin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compounds of 'master'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'master' should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: master-builder, master-stroke (exception: masterpiece).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'god' as second element
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'god,' when this word forms the second element of the compound, should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sun-god, rain-god (but: godsend, godson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen after 'half', 'quarter', etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Half', 'quarter', etc., combined with a noun should be followed by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: half-truth, half-tone; half-year, half-title, quarter-mile; but not the adverb 'halfway.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefixes semi-, demi-, bi-, tri- generally without hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Semi-', 'demi-', 'bi-', 'tri-', etc., do not ordinarily demand a hyphen, unless followed by i, w, or y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: semiannual, demigod, bipartisan, bichromate, bimetallist, trimonthly, tricolor; exceptions: semi-barbarous, semi-translucent and long/unusual formations. Also note forms like semi-incandescent, bi-weekly, tri-yearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'self-' compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'self,' when this word forms the first element of the compound, are hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: self-evident, self-respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations with 'fold' printed as one or two words by syllable count
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations with 'fold' are to be printed as one word if the number contains only one syllable; if it contains more, as two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: twofold, tenfold; fifteen fold, a hundred fold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives formed by suffixation of 'like' printed or hyphenated by syllable count
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives formed by the suffixation of 'like' to a noun are usually printed as one word if the noun contains only one syllable (except when ending in /); if it contains more (or is a proper noun), they should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: childlike, homelike, warlike, godlike; eel-like, bell-like; woman-like, business-like; American-like (but: Christlike).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate parts of titles (vice-, ex-, elect, general)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Vice,' 'ex-,' 'elect,' and 'general,' constituting parts of titles, should be connected with the chief noun by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vice-Consul Taylor, ex-President Cleveland, the governor-elect, the postmaster-general. Note: do not hyphenate military titles like surgeon general, lieutenant general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'by-' compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'by-' when this word forms the first element of the compound should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: by-product, by-laws (but: bygones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate co-, pre-, re- when followed by same vowel or w/y or to avoid diphthong ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: The prefixes 'co-,' 'pre-,' and 're-,' when followed by the same vowel as that in which they terminate, or by w or y, or by any letter that forms a diphthong with the last letter of the prefix, except in very common words, take a hyphen; but as a rule they do not when followed by a different vowel or by a consonant, except to avoid mispronunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: co-operation, pre-empted, re-enter, co-worker, re-yield; but: coequal, coeducation, prearranged, reinstall; exceptions include proper names, long/unusual words, and cases where omission changes meaning: pre-Raphaelite, re-democratize, re-pulverization; re-cover (cover again) vs recover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit hyphen from today/tomorrow/tonight/viewpoint/standpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the hyphen from 'today,' 'tomorrow,' 'tonight,' 'viewpoint,' 'standpoint.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 119 note for related matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative particles un-, in-, il-, im-, a- usually without hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: The negative particles 'un-,' 'in-,' 'il-,' 'im-,' and 'a-' do not usually require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unmanly, undemocratic, inanimate, indeterminate, illimitable, impersonal, asymmetrical. Exceptions rare/artificial combinations. The particle 'non-' ordinarily calls for a hyphen except in the commonest words: non-aesthetic, non-subservient, non-contagious ... but: nonage, nondescript, nonessential, nonsense, noncombatant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'quasi-' prefixed nouns/adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Quasi-' prefixed to a noun or an adjective requires a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quasi-corporation, quasi-historical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not hyphenate over-/under- prefixes except unusual cases
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Over' and 'under' prefixed to a word should not be followed by a hyphen, except in unusual cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: overbold, overemphasize, overweight, underfed, underestimate, undersecretary; but: over-soul, under-man, over-spiritualistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin/Greek preposition prefixes usually without hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: The Latin prepositions ante, infra, inter, intra, post, sub, super, supra, and the Greek preposition anti prefixed to a word do not ordinarily require a hyphen, unless followed by the letter with which they terminate, or, in the case of those prefixes ending in a vowel, by -w, by -y, or by a vowel which would form a diphthong in conjunction with the terminal letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: antedate, antechamber, antediluvian, inframarginal, international, interstate, intramural, postscript, postgraduate, postprandial, subconscious, submarine, subtitle, subway, superfine, supraliminal, antidote, antiseptic. Exceptions: ante-bellum, ante-Nicene, anti-Semitic, inter-university, post-revolutionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen with extra-, pan-, ultra- generally
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Extra,' 'pan,' and 'ultra' as a rule call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: extra-hazardous, pan-Hellenic, ultra-conservative (but: extraordinary, Ultramontane).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen in spelled-out fractional numbers between numerator and denominator
rubrics_metrics.description: In fractional numbers, spelled out, connect by a hyphen the numerator and the denominator, unless either already contains a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The year is two-thirds gone'; four and five-sevenths; thirty one-hundredths; but: thirty-one hundredths. Do not hyphenate in constructions like 'One half of his fortune he bequeathed to his widow; the other, to charitable institutions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen to indicate omitted common element in series of compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more compound words occurring together have one component element in common, that element is frequently omitted from all but the last word, and its implication should be indicated by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: English- and Spanish-speaking countries; one-, five-, and ten-cent pieces; literary example: 'fifth- and tenth-century Europe.' Note some regard this hyphen as objectionable Teutonism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen to indicate prefix or suffix particle
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is used to indicate a prefix or a suffix, as a particle or syllable, not complete in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The prefix a-'; 'The Spanish diminutive suffixes -ito and -cita.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen to indicate syllables
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is employed to indicate the syllables of a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: di-a-gram, pho-tog-ra-phy.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of common everyday words to hyphenate
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of words of everyday occurrence that should be hyphenated and do not fall under earlier classifications is provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: after-years, death-rate, anti-trust, first-fruits, bas-relief, folk-song, birth-rate, horse-power, blood-feud, ice-cream, blood-relations, loan-word, coat-of-arms, man-of-war, cross-reference, mid-year, object-lesson, title-page, page-proof, trade-mark, pay-roll, wave-length, poor-law, well-being, sea-level, well-nigh, sense-perception, well-wisher, subject-matter, will-power, thought-process. Otherwise Webster's Dictionary is standard for many compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary word divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid all unnecessary divisions of words. Wherever consistent with good spacing, carry the whole word over into the next line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General instruction to minimize hyphenation at line-ends when spacing permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dividing very short syllables in wide measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not, in wide measures (20 ems or more), divide on a syllable of two letters, if possible to avoid it. Never carry over a syllable of two letters. Words of four letters should never be divided; words of five or six rarely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance for typesetting in wide measure; good spacing is paramount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit consecutive lines ending in hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: Never let more than two consecutive lines terminate in a hyphen, if at all avoidable. The next to the last line in a paragraph ought not to end in a divided word; the last line (the 'breakline') should, in measures of 15 ems and up, contain at least four letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also avoid divided words at bottom of a recto page when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide proper nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide proper nouns, especially names of persons, unless absolutely necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful avoidance of splitting personal names across lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not separate initials or certain combinations across lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not separate (put in different lines) the initials of a name, or combinations like 1496 A.D., 6:00 P.M., £6 43. 6d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep initialisms and such notations intact on one line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep divisional mark with the matter it precedes
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the separation of a divisional mark, e.g., (a) or (i), in the middle of a sentence from the section which it precedes; i.e., do not allow such a mark to fall at the end of a line, but carry it over with the matter to which it pertains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typesetting rule to keep enumeration markers with their following text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide according to pronunciation (American system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide according to pronunciation (the American system), not according to derivation (the English system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: democ-racy (not demo-cracy); knowl-edge (not know-ledge); aurif-erous (not auri-ferous); antip-odes (better antipo-des). However, where compatible with pronunciation and spacing, divide compounds on etymological lines: dis-pleasure better than displeas-ure; school-master than schoolmas-ter. Never divide on syllables with a silent vowel: possi-ble, vex-ed, enti-tled, princi-ples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide between consonants when syllable ends on one consonant
rubrics_metrics.description: When two consonants meet between vowels, and the syllable ends on one consonant, the division may properly be made between the consonants, the pronunciation determining the place of division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: advan-tage, exces-sive, finan-cier, foun-da-tion, impor-tant, In-dian, moun-tain, profes-sor, struc-ture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid line-ending divisions creating awkward consonant endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not terminate a line in a soft c or gy or in a j. Escape the division entirely if possible; if not, divide appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pro-cess, not proc-ess; ne-cessary, not nec-essary; spacing rule that present participle -ing should be carried over. Note difference from Webster's rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide on a vowel when practicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel wherever practicable. In case a vowel alone forms a syllable in the middle of a word, run it into the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sepa-rate (not sep-arate); particu-lar (not partic-ular). Exceptions: words in -able and -ible should carry the vowel over into the next line: read-able, not reada-ble; convert-ible, not converti-ble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid additional hyphens in hyphenated nouns/adjectives when dividing
rubrics_metrics.description: In hyphenated nouns and adjectives avoid additional hyphens when dividing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: object-lesson, not object-les-son; fellow-being, not fel-low-being; poverty-stricken, not pov-erty-stricken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat vowel diphthongs as single letters for division
rubrics_metrics.description: A coalition of two vowel-sounds into one (i.e., a diphthong) should be treated as one letter. Therefore do not divide such combinations across lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: do not divide peo-ple (either syllable makes a bad division), Cae-sar (cf. 218), bu-ilding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry t with suffix when accent shifts in derivatives from words ending in t
rubrics_metrics.description: In derivatives from words ending in t, the t in divisions should be carried into the next line with the suffix if the accent has been shifted; if the derivative has retained the accent of the parent-word, the t should be left in the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: objec-tive (from ob'ject); defect-ive (from defect'); but: respec-tively, distinc-tive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural s does not justify additional division for s-sound endings
rubrics_metrics.description: The addition of a plural s, adding a new syllable to words ending in an s-sound, does not create a new excuse for dividing such words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hor-ses and circumstan-ces are impossible divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives in -ical should be divided on the i
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives in -ical should be divided on the i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: physi-cal, not phys-ical nor physic-al.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide 'nothing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literal admonition to avoid nonsensical divisions; likely means avoid dividing the word 'nothing' or avoid leaving nothing as a fragment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensed rules for dividing foreign-language words
rubrics_metrics.description: Condensed rules for dividing words in the foreign languages most frequently met with in proofreading (French, German, Italian, Spanish, Greek, Latin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers language-specific syllabification and division rules; see subsequent entries for per-language specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: French division: divide on a vowel where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental principle: divide on a vowel as far as possible, avoiding consonantal ending of syllables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in-di-vi-si-bi-li-te, a-che-ter; tableau (not tab-leau); balancer (not bal-ancer).

rubrics_metrics.name: French division: carry certain consonant pairs over
rubrics_metrics.description: Two consonants of which the second is l or r (but not rl, lr) are both carried over to the following syllable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ta-bleau, e-cri-vain, per-dre, qua-tre; par-ler, hur-ler.

rubrics_metrics.name: French division: vowel count principle and mute e rule
rubrics_metrics.description: There are as many syllables as there are vowels, even if soundless; but a mute e following a vowel does not form a syllable; certain letters before vowels often sound as consonants and then do not form a syllable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: par-lent, vic-toi-re, pro-pri-e'-tai-re, guer-re, filles; but e-taient, joue-rai; and mie i, yeux, loin, fouet-ter, e-cuel-le examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: German division: divide on a vowel where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental principle: divide on a vowel as far as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hi-lten, le-ben, Fa-brik.

rubrics_metrics.name: German division: carry only last consonant when several between vowels
rubrics_metrics.description: If several consonants stand between vowels, usually only the last is carried over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Rit-ter, klir-ren, Klemp-ner, Ver-wand-te, Karp-fen.

rubrics_metrics.name: German division: certain consonant clusters never separated
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations sz, ch, sch, ph, st, th are never separated (with noted exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Busze, Be-cher, Ha-scher (but: Haus-chen), Geo-gra-phie, La-sten, Ma-thilde.

rubrics_metrics.name: German division: ck separated into k-k when divided
rubrics_metrics.description: If ck must be divided, it is separated into k-k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Deckel — Dek-kel.

rubrics_metrics.name: German division: foreign words carry certain consonant combos over
rubrics_metrics.description: In foreign words (Fremdwörter), combinations of b, d, g, k, p, t with l or r are carried over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Publikum, Metrum, Hydrant (Pu-bli-kum, Me-trum, Hy-drant).

rubrics_metrics.name: German division: compound words separated into elements then divided
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound words are separated first into their component elements, and within each element the foregoing rules apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Fürsten-schloss, Tur-an-gel, Interesse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italian division: divide on a vowel where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental principle: divide on a vowel as far as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ta-vo-li-no, nar-ra-re.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italian division: certain consonant clusters and letter groups never separated
rubrics_metrics.description: s before a consonant, r following a consonant, ch, gh, gli (gl), gn, qu, sc, and others are never separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ca-sti-ghi, av-ro, migliori, bisogno, inchiostro, uscire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italian division: i and u with following vowels treated as consonants; certain digraphs not separated
rubrics_metrics.description: i=y and u=w go with the following vowel; ac, au, ei, eu, oi are not separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: miei, tuoi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish division: divide on a vowel where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental principle: divide on a vowel as far as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ca-ra-co-les, re-ba-no, fle-xi-bi-li-dad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish division: treat certain consonant clusters as simple consonants
rubrics_metrics.description: br, bl, ch, cl, cr, dr, ll, pr, rr, tr, and ñ, being regarded as simple consonants, follow the vowel-division rule; cc and nn are divided as in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: muchacho, batalla, bu-ilo, barrio, cigarro; ac-ceso, en-no-ble-cer, in-ne-ga-ble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish division: liquid consonants rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The liquid consonants l and r, when preceded by any consonant other than s, must not be separated from that consonant, except in uniting parts of compound words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hablar, podria, celebra-cion, siglo; but sub-lu-nar, sub-ra-yar, es-la-bon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish division: separable consonants should be divided; s disjoined from following consonant
rubrics_metrics.description: Two separable consonants should be divided; s is always disjoined from a following consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cuer-da, chas-co, pron-to; has-ta, as-pi-rar, cons-pi-rar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek division: place certain consonants at beginning of syllable
rubrics_metrics.description: Single consonants, combinations which can begin a word, and mutes followed by p or b are placed at the beginning of a syllable; other combinations of consonants are divided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given in Greek script (syllabification examples). Compound words are divided into original parts, then rules apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek division: compound words divided into original parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound words are divided into their original parts; subject to that, the general Greek division rules apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in Greek script: compounds such as t rpo[r]-a-...]

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin division: vowel/diphthong syllable counting
rubrics_metrics.description: A Latin word has as many syllables as it has vowels or diphthongs (ae, au, oe, ei, eu, ui).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base principle for Latin syllabification and division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin division: single consonant between vowels divides before the consonant
rubrics_metrics.description: When a single consonant occurs between two vowels, divide before the consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cae-sar, me-ri-di-es.
